{{short description|German mathematician}}
'''Hans Ludwig Hamburger''' (5 August 1889, [[Berlin]] – 14 August 1956, [[Cologne]]) was a German [[mathematician]]. He was a professor at the [[Friedrich Wilhelm University of Berlin]], the [[University of Cologne]], and [[Ankara University]].<ref name="grimshaw">{{citation | last=Grimshaw | first=M. E. | title=Hans Ludwig Hamburger | journal=[[Journal of the London Mathematical Society|J. London Math. Soc.]] |date=July 1958 | volume=33 | issue=3 | pages=377–383 | doi=10.1112/jlms/s1-33.3.377 | mr=98650 | zbl = 0080.00404 }}.</ref>

==Biography==
Hans was the elder son of Karl Hamburger and Margarethe Levy. He was of Jewish heritage, but baptised as a protestant.<ref name="HMA">{{cite web|last1=O'Connor|first1=J J|last2=Robertson|first2=E F|title=Hans Ludwig Hamburger|url=http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Biographies/Hamburger.htmly.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Biographies/Hamburger.htmlww-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Biographies/Hamburger.html|website=MacTutor History of Mathematics archive|publisher=School of Mathematics and Statistics University of St Andrews, Scotland|accessdate=1 September 2017}}{{Dead link|date=January 2020 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> His father was a lawyer and mixed in learned circles in Berlin. Hans attended the [[Royal French Gymnasium]] in Berlin from 1898 to 1907. 
Hamburger obtained his Ph.D. from the [[Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München]] in 1914 under the supervision of [[Alfred Pringsheim]]<ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=53118|name=Hans Ludwig Hamburger}}</ref> and after war service obtained his [[Habilitation]] for a thesis on ''Extensions of the [[Stieltjes moment problem]]''. He was appointed [[Privatdozent]] at the [[Friedrich Wilhelm University of Berlin]] in 1921 and professor at the [[University of Cologne]] in 1926. He left Cologne in 1935, after the imposition of the [[Nuremberg Laws]], and returned to his mother's home in Berlin. In 1939, he left Germany, and from 1941 to 1946 he was lecturer at the [[University of Southampton]]. After the war, he received an invitation to return to the University of Cologne, but instead moved to [[Ankara University]] in 1947. He returned to Cologne in 1953.<ref name="grimshaw"/><ref>{{citation|title=Mathematicians fleeing from Nazi Germany: individual fates and global impact|first=Reinhard|last=Siegmund-Schultze|publisher=Princeton University Press|year=2009|isbn=978-0-691-14041-4|pages=115, 324}}.</ref>

He was married briefly twice, to Malla Jessen in 1927 and to Vera Schereschevsky two months prior to his death in 1956.<ref name="grimshaw"/>

==Research==
The main results from Hamburger's pre-war research concerned the [[Hamburger moment problem]], which is named after him, and his work on the [[Carathéodory conjecture]], beginning in Berlin in 1922.<ref name="grimshaw"/> His work on this topic was published only 20 years later, a reflection of the difficulty of the problem. He attributed the conjecture to [[Constantin Carathéodory|Carathéodory]] and his approach was a reformulation of the conjecture in terms of a bound on the index of an isolated [[umbilic point]] of a surface. His attribution remains in place today, and his solution of the [[Carathéodory conjecture]] in the real analytic case is regarded as complete. He also proved a [[converse theorem]] for the [[Riemann zeta function]].<ref name="grimshaw"/>

After the war, Hamburger's research primarily concerned [[linear transformation]]s of [[Hilbert space]].<ref name="grimshaw"/> Hamburger published the textbook, ''Linear Transformations in n-Dimensional Vector Space. An Introduction to the Theory of Hilbert Space (1951)'' with [[Margaret Grimshaw]].
